items.question_md:
If the weight of the members is neglected, determine the forces of the pin on the lever at $A$.

[Figure: Lever $ABC$ pinned at $A$, with a $400\,N$ horizontal force applied at $C$. $C$ is $0.5\,m$ above $B$. Short link $BD$ connects pin $B$ on the lever to support $D$, inclined at $45^\circ$, with horizontal and vertical offsets of $0.2\,m$. $A$ is $0.2\,m$ below $B$ and $0.1\,m$ horizontally from $B$.]
items.answer_md:
**Reading of the figure:** take A as origin. B is 0.1 m to the right and 0.2 m above A: $B=(0.1,\ 0.2)$. C is 0.5 m above B: $C=(0.1,\ 0.7)$. The 400 N acts horizontally at C. Link BD is at $45^\circ$, with D 0.2 m horizontally and 0.2 m vertically from B, on the side such that BD is along the line of slope $-1$ through B.

**Step 1: Free body of lever ABC.** BD is a two-force member, so its force $F_{BD}$ on the lever acts along BD. Unknowns: $F_{BD}$, $A_x$, $A_y$.

**Step 2: $\Sigma M_A=0$**
- Moment of 400 N about A: $400\times0.7=280$ N·m
- Perpendicular distance from A to line BD (slope $-1$ through B): $\dfrac{0.1+0.2}{\sqrt2}=0.2121$ m
$$F_{BD}\times0.2121=280\Rightarrow F_{BD}=1320\ \text{N}=1.32\ \text{kN}$$
Components: $F_{BD}\cos45^\circ=F_{BD}\sin45^\circ=933.3$ N.

**Step 3: Force equations** (400 N to the right; link force on the lever acting up and to the left)
$$\Sigma F_x=0:\ A_x+400-933.3=0\Rightarrow A_x=533.3\ \text{N}$$
$$\Sigma F_y=0:\ A_y+933.3=0\Rightarrow A_y=-933.3\ \text{N}\ (\text{downward})$$

**Step 4: Resultant pin force at A**
$$F_A=\sqrt{533.3^2+933.3^2}=\mathbf{1075\ N\approx1.07\ kN}$$
$$\theta=\tan^{-1}\frac{933.3}{533.3}=\mathbf{60.3^\circ}\ \text{below the horizontal}$$
($F_{BD}=1.32$ kN.)

items.path: library/archive/CE1103/Mini Test/Mini Test 2024-25 Sem 1 Section E.pdf
items.topic: Centroid of areas
items.question_md:
Find the centroid of the area bounded between the $x$-axis, the line $x = a$ and the curve $y = kx^n$, where the curve passes through the point $(a, b)$.

[Figure: Curve $y = kx^n$ from the origin to the point $(a, b)$, with the shaded area between the curve and the $x$-axis up to $x = a$; height $b$ marked at $x = a$; a vertical elemental strip of width $dx$ and height $y$ at distance $x$ from the origin.]
items.answer_md:
**Given:** $y = kx^n$ through $(a, b)$, so $b = ka^n \Rightarrow k = \dfrac{b}{a^n}$.

**Element:** vertical strip at distance $x$, width $dx$, height $y = kx^n$: $dA = kx^n\,dx$; its centroid is at $\left(x, \dfrac{y}{2}\right)$.

**Area:**
$$A = \int_0^a kx^n\,dx = \frac{k a^{n+1}}{n+1} = \frac{ab}{n+1}$$

**Moment about the y-axis:**
$$\int x\,dA = \int_0^a kx^{n+1}\,dx = \frac{k a^{n+2}}{n+2} = \frac{a^2 b}{n+2}$$
$$\bar{x} = \frac{a^2 b/(n+2)}{ab/(n+1)} = \frac{(n+1)}{(n+2)}\,a$$

**Moment about the x-axis:**
$$\int \frac{y}{2}\,dA = \int_0^a \frac{k^2 x^{2n}}{2}\,dx = \frac{k^2 a^{2n+1}}{2(2n+1)} = \frac{a b^2}{2(2n+1)}$$
$$\bar{y} = \frac{ab^2/[2(2n+1)]}{ab/(n+1)} = \frac{(n+1)}{2(2n+1)}\,b$$

**Result:** $$\boxed{\bar{x} = \frac{n+1}{n+2}\,a, \qquad \bar{y} = \frac{n+1}{4n+2}\,b}$$

Check: $n = 1$ (triangle) gives $\bar{x} = 2a/3$, $\bar{y} = b/3$ ✓; $n = 2$ (parabolic spandrel) gives $\bar{x} = 3a/4$, $\bar{y} = 3b/10$ ✓.

items.question_md:
A square board ABCD is fixed in a vertical plane. Two pulleys P & Q on the board carry loads of 25 N & 50 N suspended by the strings. The co-ordinates of the centre of pulley are $(1,4)$ P & Q $(4,1)$ in m, respectively. Measure the magnitude & direction of the resultant & the distance from A to the action of resultant.

[Figure: Square board ABCD with A at bottom-left (origin, axes drawn through A), B bottom-right, C top-right, D top-left. Pulley P at $(1,4)$ near the top and pulley Q at $(4,1)$. A string passes from point F (on the left, inclined at $60^\circ$ to the horizontal) over the pulley(s) to point E (top right, inclined at $30^\circ$ to the horizontal). Loads of 25 N and 50 N hang vertically from pulleys P and Q respectively.]
items.answer_md:
**Reading of the figure (assumption):** each pulley carries its own string. At P the string carries 25 N (the hanging load) and its other part runs to F, down and to the left at $60^\circ$ to the horizontal. At Q the string carries 50 N and its other part runs to E, up and to the right at $30^\circ$. Over a smooth pulley the tension is the same in both parts, and the pulley transmits both tensions to the board through its centre.

**Axes:** origin at A, x along AB, y along AD; P(1, 4), Q(4, 1) in m.

### 1. Forces on the board
| At | Force | $F_x$ (N) | $F_y$ (N) |
|---|---|---|---|
| P | 25 N vertical load | 0 | −25 |
| P | 25 N towards F at $60^\circ$ | $-25\cos60^\circ = -12.50$ | $-25\sin60^\circ = -21.65$ |
| Q | 50 N vertical load | 0 | −50 |
| Q | 50 N towards E at $30^\circ$ | $50\cos30^\circ = 43.30$ | $50\sin30^\circ = 25.00$ |
| | **Sum** | **30.80** | **−71.65** |

### 2. Resultant
$$R = \sqrt{30.80^2 + 71.65^2} = \mathbf{77.99\ N}$$
$$\theta = \tan^{-1}\frac{71.65}{30.80} = \mathbf{66.74^\circ}\ \text{below the horizontal, acting down and to the right}$$

### 3. Moment about A ($M = xF_y - yF_x$, anticlockwise positive)
- At P: $1(-46.65) - 4(-12.50) = +3.35$ N·m
- At Q: $4(-25.00) - 1(43.30) = -143.30$ N·m

$$\sum M_A = -139.95\ \text{N·m (clockwise)}$$

### 4. Distance from A
$$d = \frac{139.95}{77.99} = \mathbf{1.79\ m}\ \text{(perpendicular distance)}$$
The line of action cuts AB at $x = 139.95/71.65 = 1.95$ m from A.

If the strings in your figure run in other directions, keep the same table: change only the angles and signs of the inclined tensions.

items.topic: Centroid of areas
items.question_md:
A thin wire of homogeneous material is bent to form an isosceles ABC. Determine the base angle $\theta$ for which the centre of weight of wire coincides with the centroid of the area enclosed by the wire.

[Figure: Isosceles triangle ABC with apex A at top, base BC of length $2l$ with midpoint O, base angles $\theta$ at B and C, height $h$.]
items.answer_md:
**Given:** isosceles triangle ABC, base BC = $2l$ with mid-point O, base angles $\theta$, height $h = l\tan\theta$. Each inclined side AB = AC = $L = \dfrac{l}{\cos\theta}$. Take O as origin, y-axis along OA (axis of symmetry), so both centroids lie on OA.

**Centroid of the enclosed area (triangle):** $\bar{y}_{area} = \dfrac{h}{3}$ above the base.

**Centre of gravity of the wire** (three straight segments, each with its centre at its mid-point):

| Segment | Length | $y$ of its centre |
|---|---|---|
| BC | $2l$ | 0 |
| AB | $L$ | $h/2$ |
| AC | $L$ | $h/2$ |

$$\bar{y}_{wire} = \frac{2l(0) + 2L(h/2)}{2l + 2L} = \frac{L h}{2(l + L)}$$

**Condition:** $\bar{y}_{wire} = \bar{y}_{area}$
$$\frac{L h}{2(l + L)} = \frac{h}{3} \Rightarrow 3L = 2l + 2L \Rightarrow L = 2l$$
$$\frac{l}{\cos\theta} = 2l \Rightarrow \cos\theta = \frac{1}{2}$$

$$\boxed{\theta = 60^\circ}$$
The triangle must be equilateral.

items.path: library/archive/CE1103/Mini Test/Mini Test 2024-25 Sem 2 Section H.pdf
items.topic: Equilibrium of rigid bodies in two and three dimensions
items.question_md:
A uniform rod AB of weight 270 N and length equal to 3 meter is hinged at point A. At point B a weight of 120 N is hung. The rod is kept in horizontal position by a string BC which makes an angle of $30^\circ$ with the rod. Find the tension in the string and the reaction at A.

[Figure: Horizontal rod AB of length 3 m, hinged to a wall at A on the left. A string runs from end B up and to the left to a fixed support at C, making an angle of $30^\circ$ with the rod at B. A weight of 120 N hangs from B.]
items.answer_md:
**Given:** uniform rod AB, $L = 3$ m, self-weight $W = 270$ N acting at its mid-point (1.5 m from A), load 120 N at B, string BC at $30^\circ$ to the rod, hinge at A.

**To find:** tension $T$ in BC and reaction $R_A$ at A.

### 1. Free body diagram of AB
- At A (hinge): unknown components $H_A$ (horizontal) and $V_A$ (vertical).
- 270 N downward at 1.5 m from A.
- 120 N downward at B (3 m from A).
- Tension $T$ at B along BC, towards C (up and towards the wall). Components: $T\cos30^\circ$ horizontal (towards A), $T\sin30^\circ$ vertical (upward).

### 2. Moments about A ($\sum M_A = 0$)
The horizontal component of $T$ passes through A (rod is horizontal), so only $T\sin30^\circ$ has a moment:
$$T\sin30^\circ \times 3 = 270 \times 1.5 + 120 \times 3 = 405 + 360 = 765\ \text{N·m}$$
$$T = \frac{765}{3 \times 0.5} = \mathbf{510\ N}$$

### 3. Horizontal equilibrium ($\sum F_x = 0$)
$$H_A = T\cos30^\circ = 510 \times 0.866 = 441.67\ \text{N}$$
acting away from the wall (opposing the horizontal pull of the string).

### 4. Vertical equilibrium ($\sum F_y = 0$)
$$V_A + T\sin30^\circ = 270 + 120 \Rightarrow V_A = 390 - 255 = 135\ \text{N (upward)}$$

### 5. Resultant reaction at A
$$R_A = \sqrt{H_A^2 + V_A^2} = \sqrt{441.67^2 + 135^2} = \mathbf{461.84\ N}$$
$$\theta = \tan^{-1}\frac{V_A}{H_A} = \tan^{-1}\frac{135}{441.67} = \mathbf{17.0^\circ}\ \text{with the horizontal}$$

**Answer:** $T = 510$ N; $R_A = 461.84$ N acting at $17.0^\circ$ to the rod, directed upward and away from the wall.

items.path: library/archive/CE1103/Previous Year End Term Papers/End Term 2020-21.pdf
items.topic: Composition of concurrent forces in a plane
items.question_md: State and prove parallelogram law of forces?
items.answer_md:
**Statement:** If two forces acting at a point are represented in magnitude and direction by the two adjacent sides of a parallelogram, their resultant is represented in magnitude and direction by the diagonal of the parallelogram through that point.

For forces P and Q at angle $\theta$:
$$R=\sqrt{P^2+Q^2+2PQ\cos\theta},\qquad \tan\alpha=\frac{Q\sin\theta}{P+Q\cos\theta}$$
where $\alpha$ is the angle of R with P.

**Proof:** in parallelogram OACB, OA = P, OB = AC = Q, $\angle AOB=\theta$, so $\angle CAD=\theta$. Drop CD perpendicular to OA produced: $AD=Q\cos\theta$, $CD=Q\sin\theta$. In right triangle OCD:
$$OC^2=(OA+AD)^2+CD^2=(P+Q\cos\theta)^2+(Q\sin\theta)^2=P^2+Q^2+2PQ\cos\theta$$
and $\tan\alpha=\dfrac{CD}{OD}=\dfrac{Q\sin\theta}{P+Q\cos\theta}$.

items.path: library/archive/CE1103/Previous Year End Term Papers/End Term 2020-21.pdf
items.topic: Composition of concurrent forces in a plane
items.question_md: Distinguish clearly between resolution of forces and composition of forces?
items.answer_md:
| Composition of forces | Resolution of forces |
|---|---|
| The process of finding a **single resultant** force that replaces two or more forces. | The process of **splitting a single force** into two or more components. |
| Many forces → one force. | One force → many (usually two perpendicular) components. |
| Done by parallelogram law, triangle law, polygon law or analytically: $R=\sqrt{(\Sigma F_x)^2+(\Sigma F_y)^2}$, $\tan\theta=\Sigma F_y/\Sigma F_x$. | Components along x and y: $F_x=F\cos\theta$, $F_y=F\sin\theta$. |
| The result is unique. | Components depend on the chosen directions (infinitely many sets possible). |
| *Example:* finding the resultant of 3 forces acting on a hook. | *Example:* a 100 N pull at $30^\circ$ gives $86.6$ N horizontal and $50$ N vertical. |

The two are inverse operations; in the analytical method each force is first resolved and the components are then composed into the resultant.

items.topic: Composition of concurrent forces in a plane
items.question_md:
The following forces act at a point:

(i) 20 N inclined at $30^\circ$ towards North of East.

(ii) 25 N towards North.

(iii) 30 N towards North West and

(iv) 35 N inclined at $40^\circ$ towards South of west.

Find the magnitude and direction of resultant force.
items.answer_md:
**Given (angles measured anticlockwise from East):**

| Force | Direction | Angle | $F_x$ (N) | $F_y$ (N) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 20 N | $30^\circ$ North of East | $30^\circ$ | 17.321 | 10.000 |
| 25 N | North | $90^\circ$ | 0 | 25.000 |
| 30 N | North-West | $135^\circ$ | $-21.213$ | 21.213 |
| 35 N | $40^\circ$ South of West | $220^\circ$ | $-26.812$ | $-22.498$ |
| **Sum** | | | **$-30.704$** | **33.716** |

**Resultant:**
$$R=\sqrt{(-30.704)^2+33.716^2}=\mathbf{45.60\ N}$$
$$\theta=\tan^{-1}\frac{33.716}{30.704}=47.68^\circ$$
$\Sigma F_x$ negative, $\Sigma F_y$ positive, so R is in the second quadrant: **R = 45.60 N acting at $47.68^\circ$ North of West** (i.e. $132.32^\circ$ anticlockwise from East).

items.topic: Equilibrium of rigid bodies in two and three dimensions
items.question_md: State and prove Lami's Theorem.
items.answer_md:
### Statement
If three coplanar forces acting at a point are in equilibrium, each force is proportional to the sine of the angle between the other two.
$$\frac{P}{\sin\alpha} = \frac{Q}{\sin\beta} = \frac{R}{\sin\gamma}$$
where $\alpha$ = angle between Q and R, $\beta$ = angle between R and P, $\gamma$ = angle between P and Q.

### Proof
1. Let P, Q, R act at point O and keep it in equilibrium (sketch: three arrows from O with angles $\gamma$ between P and Q, $\alpha$ between Q and R, $\beta$ between R and P; $\alpha + \beta + \gamma = 360^\circ$).
2. Complete the parallelogram OACB on P (along OA) and Q (along OB). The diagonal OC is the resultant of P and Q.
3. For equilibrium, R must be equal and opposite to this resultant, so R lies along CO produced and $OC = R$.
4. In triangle OAC: $OA = P$, $AC = OB = Q$, $OC = R$.
   - $\angle AOC = 180^\circ - \beta$ (since R is opposite OC and makes $\beta$ with P)
   - $\angle ACO = \angle COB = 180^\circ - \alpha$
   - $\angle OAC = 180^\circ - \gamma$
5. Sine rule in triangle OAC:
$$\frac{OA}{\sin\angle ACO} = \frac{AC}{\sin\angle AOC} = \frac{OC}{\sin\angle OAC}$$
$$\frac{P}{\sin(180^\circ-\alpha)} = \frac{Q}{\sin(180^\circ-\beta)} = \frac{R}{\sin(180^\circ-\gamma)}$$
6. Since $\sin(180^\circ - \theta) = \sin\theta$:
$$\mathbf{\frac{P}{\sin\alpha} = \frac{Q}{\sin\beta} = \frac{R}{\sin\gamma}}$$
Hence proved.

items.topic: Equilibrium of rigid bodies in two and three dimensions
items.question_md:
Two smooth spheres of weight W and radius r each are in equilibrium in a horizontal channel of A and B vertical sides as shown figure. Find the force exerted by each sphere on the other, if $r = 250$ mm, $b = 900$ mm and $W = 100$ N.

[Figure: Two spheres A (upper) and B (lower), each of weight W and radius r, in a channel with vertical walls a distance b apart; sphere B rests on the channel floor against the left wall, sphere A rests on sphere B against the right wall.]
items.answer_md:
**Given:** $W = 100$ N, $r = 250$ mm, channel width $b = 900$ mm, smooth surfaces.

### 1. Geometry
Horizontal distance between centres $= b - 2r = 900 - 500 = 400$ mm. Distance between centres (spheres touch) $= 2r = 500$ mm. If $\theta$ is the angle of the line of centres with the horizontal:
$$\cos\theta = \frac{400}{500} = 0.8,\qquad \sin\theta = 0.6\ (\theta = 36.87^\circ)$$

### 2. Upper sphere A
Forces: W down, wall reaction $R_w$ horizontal, contact force R from B along the line of centres.
$$\sum F_y = 0:\ R\sin\theta = W \Rightarrow R = \frac{100}{0.6} = \mathbf{166.67\ N}$$
$$\sum F_x = 0:\ R_w = R\cos\theta = 166.67 \times 0.8 = 133.33\ \text{N}$$

### 3. Lower sphere B
Floor reaction $= W + R\sin\theta = 200$ N; left wall reaction $= R\cos\theta = 133.33$ N.

**Answer:** each sphere presses on the other with **166.67 N** along the line of centres (wall reactions 133.33 N each, floor reaction 200 N).

items.topic: Perpendicular axis theorem
items.question_md: Prove the perpendicular axis theorem in the determination of moment of inertia of areas with the help of neat sketch.
items.answer_md:
**Statement:** The moment of inertia of a plane area about an axis perpendicular to its plane (Z-Z) through a point O is equal to the sum of its moments of inertia about two mutually perpendicular axes X-X and Y-Y lying in the plane and intersecting at O:
$$I_{ZZ}=I_{XX}+I_{YY}$$

**Sketch (described):** a plane lamina in the x-y plane with axes OX and OY in its plane; OZ perpendicular to the plane at O. An element $dA$ at P$(x, y)$ is at distance $r$ from O, with $r^2=x^2+y^2$.

**Proof:**
$$I_{ZZ}=\int r^2\,dA=\int (x^2+y^2)\,dA=\int x^2\,dA+\int y^2\,dA=I_{YY}+I_{XX}$$
$$\mathbf{I_{ZZ}=I_{XX}+I_{YY}}$$
*Example:* circle, $I_{ZZ}=\frac{\pi d^4}{32}$, so $I_{XX}=I_{YY}=\frac{\pi d^4}{64}$.

items.path: library/archive/CE1103/Previous Year End Term Papers/End Term 2020-21.pdf
items.topic: Moment of inertia of composite areas
items.question_md:
Find the moment of inertia of the lamina with a circular hole of 30 mm diameter above the axis AB as shown in figure below.

[Figure: Lamina with horizontal axis AB of length 60 mm (30 mm + 30 mm either side of the centre); a semicircle of radius 30 mm lies below AB, and a right triangle lies above AB with its vertical side of 60 mm at B rising to apex C; a circular hole of 30 mm diameter is centred at the midpoint of AB.]
items.answer_md:
**Given (mm):** AB = 60 mm; semicircle of radius 30 mm below AB (diameter AB); right triangle above AB with base AB = 60 and vertical side BC = 60; circular hole $d=30$ mm centred at the midpoint of AB.

**To find:** $I_{AB}$ of the lamina.

**Step 1: Semicircle about its diameter AB**
$$I_1=\frac{\pi r^4}{8}=\frac{\pi(30)^4}{8}=318086.3\ \text{mm}^4$$

**Step 2: Triangle about its base AB**
$$I_2=\frac{bh^3}{12}=\frac{60\times60^3}{12}=1080000\ \text{mm}^4$$

**Step 3: Hole about AB** (AB is a diameter of the hole)
$$I_3=\frac{\pi d^4}{64}=\frac{\pi(30)^4}{64}=39760.8\ \text{mm}^4$$
(The hole lies wholly inside the lamina: the hypotenuse AC is $30/\sqrt2=21.2$ mm from the hole's centre, more than its 15 mm radius.)

**Step 4: Lamina**
$$I_{AB}=I_1+I_2-I_3=318086.3+1080000-39760.8$$
$$\mathbf{I_{AB}=1.358\times10^6\ mm^4\ (1358325\ mm^4)}$$

items.path: library/archive/CE1103/Previous Year End Term Papers/End Term 2020-21.pdf
items.question_md: What are various type of loadings? Distinguish clearly between uniformly distributed load, uniformly varying load and triangular load.
items.answer_md:
**Types of loading on beams:**
1. **Concentrated (point) load:** acts at a single point (e.g. 10 kN at mid-span).
2. **Uniformly distributed load (UDL):** spread over a length at constant intensity $w$ (kN/m).
3. **Uniformly varying load (UVL):** intensity varies linearly along the length (triangular or trapezoidal).
4. **Applied couple / moment** at a point.

**Distinction:**
| | UDL | Uniformly varying load | Triangular load |
|---|---|---|---|
| Intensity | constant $w$ throughout | changes linearly from $w_1$ to $w_2$ | linear from zero at one end to $w$ at the other |
| Shape of load diagram | rectangle | trapezium (or triangle) | triangle |
| Total load | $wL$ | $\frac{(w_1 + w_2)}{2}L$ | $\frac{1}{2}wL$ |
| Acts at | $L/2$ (centre) | centroid of the trapezium | $L/3$ from the larger end ($2L/3$ from zero end) |
| Example | self-weight of a uniform beam | earth pressure on an inclined wall | water pressure on a vertical wall |

A triangular load is the special case of a uniformly varying load in which the intensity at one end is zero.

items.topic: Equilibrium of rigid bodies in two and three dimensions
items.question_md:
Find the support reaction of the following beam

[Figure: Beam AB of span 10 m, hinged at A and roller-supported at B; a uniformly distributed load of 20 kN/m acts over AC = 4 m; a point load of 10 kN acts at D, with CD = 4 m and DB = 2 m.]
items.answer_md:
**Given:** span AB = 10 m, hinge at A, roller at B. UDL 20 kN/m over AC = 4 m; point load 10 kN at D, where AD = AC + CD = 4 + 4 = 8 m (DB = 2 m).

### 1. FBD and equivalent loads
- UDL → $20 \times 4 = 80$ kN acting at the centre of AC, 2 m from A.
- 10 kN at 8 m from A.
- Reactions: $H_A$, $V_A$ at the hinge; $R_B$ vertical at the roller.

### 2. Horizontal equilibrium
No horizontal load acts, so $H_A = 0$.

### 3. $\sum M_A = 0$ (clockwise positive)
$$R_B \times 10 = 80 \times 2 + 10 \times 8 = 160 + 80 = 240$$
$$R_B = \mathbf{24\ kN}\ (\uparrow)$$

### 4. $\sum F_y = 0$
$$V_A = (80 + 10) - 24 = \mathbf{66\ kN}\ (\uparrow)$$

### 5. Check: $\sum M_B = 0$
$$V_A \times 10 = 80 \times 8 + 10 \times 2 = 640 + 20 = 660 \Rightarrow V_A = 66\ \text{kN}\ ✓$$

**Answer:** $R_A = 66$ kN (vertical, $H_A = 0$), $R_B = 24$ kN.

items.path: library/archive/CE1103/Previous Year End Term Papers/End Term 2020-21.pdf
items.question_md: What are the assumptions made, while finding out the forces in the various members of a framed structure?
items.answer_md:
**Assumptions made in finding forces in the members of a perfect frame:**
1. The frame is a **perfect frame** ($m = 2j - 3$).
2. All joints are **pin (hinge) joints**, frictionless, so no moment is transmitted.
3. Loads act **only at the joints**.
4. Members are straight and carry only **axial force** (tension or compression).
5. **Self-weight** of members is negligible.

items.path: library/archive/CE1103/Previous Year End Term Papers/End Term 2020-21.pdf
items.topic: Method of joints
items.question_md: State and explain the analytical methods for finding out the forces in perfect frame?
items.answer_md:
The two analytical methods for a perfect frame are:

1. **Method of joints:** each joint is isolated as a free body; the member forces and loads at the joint form a concurrent system, so $\sum F_x = 0$ and $\sum F_y = 0$ are applied. Start at a joint with only two unknowns and proceed joint by joint.
2. **Method of sections:** the frame is cut by a section through **not more than three** members whose forces are unknown; one part is taken as a free body and $\sum F_x = 0$, $\sum F_y = 0$, $\sum M = 0$ are applied. Best for finding forces in a few chosen members directly.

(A tension force pulls away from the joint, a compression force pushes towards it.)

items.path: library/archive/CE1103/Previous Year End Term Papers/End Term 2020-21.pdf
items.question_md: Define the terms Shear force and Bending Moment?
items.answer_md:
**Shear force** at a section is the algebraic sum of all vertical forces (loads and reactions) acting on either side of the section (unit: kN).

**Bending moment** at a section is the algebraic sum of the moments, about that section, of all forces acting on either side of it (unit: kN·m). Sagging BM is positive, hogging negative.

items.path: library/archive/CE1103/Previous Year End Term Papers/End Term 2020-21.pdf
items.question_md: What do you understand by the term, 'point of contraflexure'?
items.answer_md: A **point of contraflexure** is the section of a beam where the bending moment changes sign (from sagging to hogging or vice versa), so the BM there is zero and the curvature of the beam reverses. It occurs in overhanging, fixed and continuous beams.

items.path: library/archive/CE1103/Previous Year End Term Papers/End Term 2020-21.pdf
items.question_md:
A beam 10 m long carries load as shown in figure. Draw the shear force and bending moment diagrams for the beam.

[Figure: Beam CD of length 10 m supported at A and B; overhang CA = 2 m with a 3 kN point load at C; span AB = 6 m carrying a uniformly distributed load of 2 kN/m; overhang BD = 2 m with a 5 kN point load at D.]
items.answer_md:
Take $x$ from C: A at 2 m, B at 8 m, D at 10 m. Supports at A and B.

**Reactions**

UDL $= 2 \times 6 = 12$ kN at $x = 5$ m.

$\sum M_A = 0:\; 6R_B + 3(2) = 12(3) + 5(8) \Rightarrow 6R_B = 70 \Rightarrow R_B = 11.67$ kN

$R_A = 3 + 12 + 5 - 11.67 = 8.33$ kN

**Shear force**

| Point | SF left (kN) | SF right (kN) |
|---|---|---|
| C | 0 | $-3$ |
| A | $-3$ | $-3 + 8.33 = 5.33$ |
| B | $5.33 - 12 = -6.67$ | $-6.67 + 11.67 = 5.0$ |
| D | 5.0 | 0 |

SF zero in AB at $x = 2 + 5.33/2 = 4.67$ m.

**Bending moment**
- $M_C = 0$
- $M_A = -3 \times 2 = -6$ kN·m
- At $x = 4.67$ m: $M = -3(4.67) + 8.33(2.67) - (2.67)^2 = 1.11$ kN·m (**maximum sagging**)
- $M_B = -5 \times 2 = -10$ kN·m (**maximum hogging**)
- $M_D = 0$

**Points of contraflexure** ($M = 5.333(x-2) - 6 - (x-2)^2 = 0$): $x = 3.61$ m and $x = 5.72$ m from C.

SFD: $-3$ over CA, jump to $+5.33$, line to $-6.67$ at B (zero at 4.67 m), jump to $+5$, constant to D.
BMD: line 0 to $-6$ at A, parabola through zero at 3.61 m, peak 1.11 at 4.67 m, through zero at 5.72 m, to $-10$ at B; line to 0 at D.

items.topic: Composition of concurrent forces in a plane
items.question_md: Show that the algebraic sum of the resolved part of a number of forces in a given direction, is equal to the resolved part of their resultant in the same direction?
items.answer_md:
Let forces $F_1, F_2, \dots, F_n$ act at a point at angles $\theta_1, \theta_2, \dots$ with the x-axis, and let their resultant R make angle $\alpha$ with it, so that
$$R\cos\alpha=\Sigma F_i\cos\theta_i,\qquad R\sin\alpha=\Sigma F_i\sin\theta_i$$
Resolved part of R along a direction at angle $\phi$:
$$R\cos(\alpha-\phi)=R\cos\alpha\cos\phi+R\sin\alpha\sin\phi=\Sigma F_i(\cos\theta_i\cos\phi+\sin\theta_i\sin\phi)$$
$$\mathbf{R\cos(\alpha-\phi)=\Sigma F_i\cos(\theta_i-\phi)}$$
i.e. the resolved part of the resultant in any direction equals the algebraic sum of the resolved parts of the forces in that direction.

items.topic: Composition of concurrent forces in a plane
items.question_md: The resultant of two forces $P$ and $Q$ is $R$. If $Q$ is Doubled, the new resultant is perpendicular to $P$. Prove that $Q$ is equals to $R$?
items.answer_md:
Let the angle between P and Q be $\theta$.

**Original resultant:**
$$R^2=P^2+Q^2+2PQ\cos\theta\qquad(1)$$

**When Q is doubled**, the new resultant $R'$ of P and 2Q makes angle $\alpha$ with P, where
$$\tan\alpha=\frac{2Q\sin\theta}{P+2Q\cos\theta}$$
$R'$ is perpendicular to P, so $\alpha=90^\circ$ and the denominator is zero:
$$P+2Q\cos\theta=0\ \Rightarrow\ 2PQ\cos\theta=-P^2\qquad(2)$$
(Equivalently, the component of $R'$ along P is zero.)

**Substituting (2) in (1):**
$$R^2=P^2+Q^2-P^2=Q^2$$
$$\mathbf{R=Q}\qquad\text{Hence proved.}$$

items.topic: Planar force systems
items.question_md: A horizontal line PQRS is 12 m long, where $PQ = QR = RS = 4$ m. Forces of 1000 N, 1500 N, 1000 N and 500 N act at P, Q, R and S respectively with downward direction. The lines of action of these forces make angles of $90^\circ$, $60^\circ$, $45^\circ$ and $30^\circ$ respectively with PS. Find the magnitude, direction and position of the resultant force.
items.answer_md:
**Given:** PQRS horizontal, PQ = QR = RS = 4 m. Downward forces 1000 N at P ($90^\circ$), 1500 N at Q ($60^\circ$), 1000 N at R ($45^\circ$), 500 N at S ($30^\circ$) with PS, all inclined the same way.

### 1. Components
| Force | Horizontal $F\cos\theta$ (N) | Vertical $F\sin\theta$ (N, ↓) | Distance from P (m) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1000 N, $90^\circ$ | 0 | 1000 | 0 |
| 1500 N, $60^\circ$ | 750.00 | 1299.04 | 4 |
| 1000 N, $45^\circ$ | 707.11 | 707.11 | 8 |
| 500 N, $30^\circ$ | 433.01 | 250.00 | 12 |
| **Sum** | **1890.12** | **3256.15** | |

### 2. Resultant
$$R = \sqrt{1890.12^2 + 3256.15^2} = \mathbf{3764.97\ N}$$
$$\theta = \tan^{-1}\frac{3256.15}{1890.12} = \mathbf{59.87^\circ}\ \text{with PS}$$

### 3. Position (moments about P)
Horizontal components lie along PS and have no moment about P:
$$\sum M_P = 1299.04 \times 4 + 707.11 \times 8 + 250 \times 12 = 5196.15 + 5656.85 + 3000 = 13\,853.0\ \text{N·m}$$
$$x = \frac{13\,853.0}{3256.15} = \mathbf{4.25\ m\ from\ P}$$

**Answer:** R = 3764.97 N at $59.87^\circ$ to PS, cutting PS at 4.25 m from P.

items.topic: Equilibrium of rigid bodies in two and three dimensions
items.question_md: State and prove Lami's Theorem.
items.answer_md:
**Statement:** If three coplanar concurrent forces P, Q, R acting at a point keep it in equilibrium, each force is proportional to the sine of the angle between the other two:
$$\frac{P}{\sin\alpha} = \frac{Q}{\sin\beta} = \frac{R}{\sin\gamma}$$
($\alpha$ = angle between Q and R, $\beta$ between R and P, $\gamma$ between P and Q.)

**Proof:** Since the three forces are in equilibrium, they can be drawn head to tail to form a closed triangle (triangle law). The sides are proportional to P, Q, R. The interior angle opposite side P is $(180^\circ - \alpha)$, opposite Q is $(180^\circ - \beta)$, opposite R is $(180^\circ - \gamma)$. By the sine rule,
$$\frac{P}{\sin(180^\circ-\alpha)} = \frac{Q}{\sin(180^\circ-\beta)} = \frac{R}{\sin(180^\circ-\gamma)}$$
and since $\sin(180^\circ - \theta) = \sin\theta$, Lami's theorem follows.

items.path: library/archive/CE1103/Previous Year End Term Papers/End Term 2021-22 Sem 1.pdf
items.topic: Equilibrium of rigid bodies in two and three dimensions
items.question_md:
A rope is connected between two points A and B 120 cm apart at the same level. A load of 200 N is suspended from a point C on the rope 45 cm from A, as shown in figure. Find the load, that should be suspended from the rope D 30 cm from B, which will keep the rope CD horizontal.

[Figure: Supports A and B at the same level, 120 cm apart. Rope segments AC (tension $T_1$, length 45 cm), CD (tension $T_2$, horizontal, length 60 cm) and DB (tension $T_3$, length 30 cm). Load 200 N hangs at C and load $W$ hangs at D.]
items.answer_md:
**Given:** A and B level, AB = 120 cm; AC = 45 cm, CD = 60 cm (horizontal), DB = 30 cm; 200 N at C; find W at D.

### 1. Geometry
Since CD is horizontal, C and D are at the same depth $h$ below AB. Horizontal projections must add up:
$$\sqrt{45^2 - h^2} + 60 + \sqrt{30^2 - h^2} = 120 \Rightarrow \sqrt{2025 - h^2} + \sqrt{900 - h^2} = 60$$
Subtracting the squares: $(\sqrt{2025-h^2})^2 - (\sqrt{900-h^2})^2 = 1125$, so their difference $= 1125/60 = 18.75$. Hence
$$\sqrt{2025-h^2} = 39.375,\quad \sqrt{900-h^2} = 20.625,\quad h = 21.79\ \text{cm}$$
- AC inclination: $\cos\alpha = 39.375/45 = 0.875 \Rightarrow \alpha = 28.96^\circ$
- DB inclination: $\cos\gamma = 20.625/30 = 0.6875 \Rightarrow \gamma = 46.57^\circ$

### 2. Joint C (200 N, $T_1$ along CA, $T_2$ horizontal)
$$T_1\sin\alpha = 200,\qquad T_1\cos\alpha = T_2 \Rightarrow T_2 = \frac{200}{\tan28.96^\circ} = 361.48\ \text{N}$$
$T_1 = 200/\sin28.96^\circ = 413.12$ N.

### 3. Joint D (W, $T_2$ horizontal, $T_3$ along DB)
$$T_3\cos\gamma = T_2,\qquad T_3\sin\gamma = W \Rightarrow W = T_2\tan\gamma = 361.48 \times 1.0563$$
$$\boxed{W = 381.8\ \text{N}}$$
$T_3 = 525.79$ N.

**Answer:** a load of **381.8 N** at D keeps CD horizontal ($T_1 = 413.1$ N, $T_2 = 361.5$ N, $T_3 = 525.8$ N).

items.topic: Composition of concurrent forces in a plane
items.question_md: ABCD is a square. Forces of 10, 8 and 4 units act at A in the directions AD, AC and AB respectively. Using the analytical method, determine the resultant force in magnitude and direction.
items.answer_md:
**Given:** square ABCD; forces at A: 10 along AD, 8 along AC, 4 along AB. Take A as origin, AB as the x-axis and AD as the y-axis; AC is at $45^\circ$.

**Resolving:**
$$\Sigma F_x=4+8\cos45^\circ+10\cos90^\circ=4+5.657=9.657\ \text{units}$$
$$\Sigma F_y=0+8\sin45^\circ+10=5.657+10=15.657\ \text{units}$$

**Resultant:**
$$R=\sqrt{9.657^2+15.657^2}=\mathbf{18.40\ units}$$
$$\theta=\tan^{-1}\frac{15.657}{9.657}=\mathbf{58.33^\circ}\ \text{with AB (between AC and AD)}$$

items.path: library/archive/CE1103/Previous Year End Term Papers/End Term 2021-22 Sem 1.pdf
items.topic: Composition of concurrent forces in a plane
items.question_md: ABCD is a square. Forces of 10, 8 and 4 units act at A in the directions AD, AC and AB respectively. Using the analytical method, determine the magnitude and sense of two forces along the direction AJ and AH, where J and H are the mid-points of CD and BC respectively, which together will balance the above resultant.
items.answer_md:
**Given:** square ABCD of side $a$; forces at A: 10 along AD, 8 along AC, 4 along AB. A is the origin, AB the x-axis, AD the y-axis.

**Step 1: Resultant of the given forces**
$$\Sigma F_x=4+8\cos45^\circ=9.657,\qquad \Sigma F_y=10+8\sin45^\circ=15.657$$
$$R=\sqrt{9.657^2+15.657^2}=18.40\ \text{units at }58.33^\circ\text{ to AB}$$

**Step 2: Directions of AJ and AH**
- J = mid-point of CD $=(a/2,\ a)$: AJ makes $\tan^{-1}2=63.43^\circ$ with AB; unit vector $\frac{1}{\sqrt5}(1,2)$
- H = mid-point of BC $=(a,\ a/2)$: AH makes $\tan^{-1}\frac12=26.57^\circ$ with AB; unit vector $\frac{1}{\sqrt5}(2,1)$

**Step 3: Balancing condition.** Let $P$ act along AJ and $Q$ along AH (positive = from A towards J, H). For equilibrium with R:
$$\frac{P}{\sqrt5}+\frac{2Q}{\sqrt5}+9.657=0,\qquad \frac{2P}{\sqrt5}+\frac{Q}{\sqrt5}+15.657=0$$
$$P+2Q=-21.594,\qquad 2P+Q=-35.010$$

**Step 4: Solve**
$$P=\frac{-2(35.010)+21.594}{3}=-16.14,\qquad Q=\frac{-2(21.594)+35.010}{3}=-2.73$$

**Result:** the negative signs mean the forces act opposite to AJ and AH:
- **16.14 units along JA** (from J towards A)
- **2.73 units along HA** (from H towards A)

These two forces together balance the resultant 18.40 units of the given system.

items.topic: Parallel axis theorem
items.question_md: Prove the parallel axis theorem in the determination of moment of inertia of areas with the help of neat sketch.
items.answer_md:
**Statement:** The moment of inertia of a plane area about any axis in its plane is equal to the moment of inertia about a parallel axis through its centroid plus the product of the area and the square of the distance between the two axes:
$$I_{AB}=I_G+Ah^2$$

**Sketch (described):** a plane area of total area $A$ with centroid G. Axis G-G passes through G; axis A-B is parallel to G-G at distance $h$. An elemental area $dA$ is at distance $y$ from G-G, hence at $(h+y)$ from A-B.

**Proof:**
$$I_{AB}=\int (h+y)^2\,dA=\int h^2\,dA+2h\int y\,dA+\int y^2\,dA$$
- $\int h^2\,dA=h^2A$
- $\int y^2\,dA=I_G$ (by definition)
- $\int y\,dA=A\bar y$ = first moment of area about the centroidal axis $=0$, since the distance of the centroid from its own axis is zero.

Hence
$$\mathbf{I_{AB}=I_G+Ah^2}$$
*Example:* rectangle $b\times d$ about its base: $I=\frac{bd^3}{12}+bd\left(\frac d2\right)^2=\frac{bd^3}{3}$.

items.question_md:
A uniform lamina shown in figure consists of rectangle, a circle and a triangle. Determine the centroid of the lamina. All dimensions are in mm.

[Figure: Rectangle 100 mm wide and 50 mm high; a semicircle of radius 25 mm attached to its left side (overall width 125 mm); a triangle of base 50 mm and height 50 mm sitting on the top edge at the right end, apex 25 mm from each base end; the triangle's left base corner is 50 mm from the rectangle's left edge (25 mm + 50 mm from the leftmost point of the semicircle).]
items.answer_md:
**Reference axes:** origin at the bottom of the vertical line through the leftmost point of the semicircle; x horizontal, y vertical (all in mm). The semicircle (r = 25 mm) has its diameter on the left side of the rectangle, so its centre is at (25, 25).

| Part | Area $a$ (mm²) | $x$ (mm) | $y$ (mm) | $a x$ (mm³) | $a y$ (mm³) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Rectangle 100 × 50 | 5000 | 25 + 50 = 75 | 25 | 375000 | 125000 |
| Semicircle r = 25 | $\pi(25)^2/2=981.75$ | $25-\frac{4(25)}{3\pi}=14.39$ | 25 | 14127.0 | 24543.7 |
| Triangle b = 50, h = 50 | $\frac12(50)(50)=1250$ | 75 + 25 = 100 | $50+\frac{50}{3}=66.67$ | 125000 | 83333.3 |
| **Total** | **7231.75** | | | **514127.0** | **232877.0** |

$$\bar x=\frac{\sum a x}{\sum a}=\frac{514127.0}{7231.75}=71.09\ \text{mm}$$
$$\bar y=\frac{\sum a y}{\sum a}=\frac{232877.0}{7231.75}=32.20\ \text{mm}$$

**Result:** centroid of the lamina is at **$\bar x=71.09$ mm from the leftmost point of the semicircle and $\bar y=32.20$ mm above the base** of the rectangle.

items.question_md: Find the moment of inertia of a hollow rectangular section about its centroid, if the external dimensions are 40 mm deep and 30 mm wide and internal dimensions are 25 mm deep and 15 mm wide.
items.answer_md:
**Given:** outer $B=30$ mm, $D=40$ mm; inner $b=15$ mm, $d=25$ mm (concentric). Area $=1200-375=825$ mm².

The section is symmetric, so both centroidal axes pass through the common centre.

**About the horizontal centroidal axis X-X:**
$$I_{XX}=\frac{BD^3}{12}-\frac{bd^3}{12}=\frac{30\times40^3}{12}-\frac{15\times25^3}{12}=160000-19531.25$$
$$\mathbf{I_{XX}=140468.75\ mm^4}$$

**About the vertical centroidal axis Y-Y:**
$$I_{YY}=\frac{DB^3}{12}-\frac{db^3}{12}=\frac{40\times30^3-25\times15^3}{12}=\mathbf{82968.75\ mm^4}$$

items.question_md: What are various type of loadings? Distinguish clearly between uniformly distributed load and concentrated load.
items.answer_md:
**Types of loading:** concentrated (point) load, uniformly distributed load (UDL), uniformly varying load (UVL: triangular or trapezoidal), and applied couple (moment).

| Concentrated load | Uniformly distributed load |
|---|---|
| Acts at a single point (kN) | Spread over a length at constant intensity (kN/m) |
| Gives a sudden jump in the SFD | Gives a linear (sloping) SFD |
| BMD is straight lines with a kink at the load | BMD is parabolic (second degree) |
| Example: a column resting on a beam | Example: self-weight of a beam or a slab |

For calculations a UDL $w$ over length $l$ is replaced by its resultant $wl$ acting at the midpoint of the loaded length.

items.topic: Equilibrium of rigid bodies in two and three dimensions
items.question_md: Define the term support reaction. Describe the analytical method for finding out the support reaction of a beam carrying vertical loads only
items.answer_md:
**Support reaction:** the force (and, at a fixed support, the moment) that a support develops on a beam to resist the applied loads and keep the beam in equilibrium. Its type depends on the support: a roller gives one force normal to its surface, a hinge gives a force in any direction ($H$ and $V$), a fixed support gives $H$, $V$ and a moment.

**Analytical method for vertical loads only (simply supported beam AB, span $L$):**
1. Draw the FBD: replace supports by reactions $R_A$ and $R_B$. With only vertical loads the horizontal reaction is zero.
2. Convert each UDL to a point load (intensity × length) acting at the centre of its length; a triangular load to its area acting at its centroid.
3. Take moments about A ($\sum M_A = 0$), clockwise positive:
$$R_B \times L = \sum W_i x_i \Rightarrow R_B = \frac{\sum W_i x_i}{L}$$
4. Apply $\sum F_y = 0$: $R_A = \sum W_i - R_B$.
5. Check by taking moments about B.

**Example:** span 6 m, 12 kN at 2 m from A: $R_B = 12 \times 2/6 = 4$ kN, $R_A = 12 - 4 = 8$ kN.

items.topic: Equilibrium of rigid bodies in two and three dimensions
items.question_md:
A beam ABCDEF of 7.5 m long and span 4.5 m is supported at B and E. The beam is loaded as shown in figure. Find the support reaction at the two supports

[Figure: Beam A–F; AB = 1.5 m, BC = 1.5 m, DE = 1.8 m, EF = 1.5 m, span BE = 4.5 m; supports at B and E. UDL of 9 kN/m from A to C, UDL of 3 kN/m from C to F, and a 5 kN point load at D.]
items.answer_md:
**Given:** AB = 1.5 m, BC = 1.5 m, DE = 1.8 m, EF = 1.5 m, span BE = 4.5 m, so CD = 4.5 − 1.5 − 1.8 = 1.2 m. Positions from A: B = 1.5, C = 3.0, D = 4.2, E = 6.0, F = 7.5 m.

**Equivalent point loads:**
- UDL 9 kN/m on AC: $9 \times 3 = 27$ kN at 1.5 m from A (exactly over B)
- UDL 3 kN/m on CF: $3 \times 4.5 = 13.5$ kN at $3 + 2.25 = 5.25$ m from A
- 5 kN at D (4.2 m from A)

Total load $= 27 + 13.5 + 5 = 45.5$ kN.

### $\sum M_B = 0$
$$R_E \times 4.5 = 27 \times 0 + 13.5 \times (5.25 - 1.5) + 5 \times (4.2 - 1.5)$$
$$R_E \times 4.5 = 50.625 + 13.5 = 64.125 \Rightarrow R_E = \mathbf{14.25\ kN}$$

### $\sum F_y = 0$
$$R_B = 45.5 - 14.25 = \mathbf{31.25\ kN}$$

**Check ($\sum M_E = 0$):** all loads lie left of E: $27 \times 4.5 + 13.5 \times 0.75 + 5 \times 1.8 = 121.5 + 10.125 + 9 = 140.625$ kN·m $= R_B \times 4.5 = 31.25 \times 4.5$ ✓

**Answer:** $R_B = 31.25$ kN, $R_E = 14.25$ kN (both upward).

items.question_md: State Clearly the difference between a perfect frame and an imperfect frame?
items.answer_md:
| Perfect frame | Imperfect frame |
|---|---|
| $m = 2j - 3$ | $m \neq 2j - 3$ |
| Just enough members to retain its shape under load | Fewer (deficient) or more (redundant) members than needed |
| Statically determinate; forces by statics alone | Deficient: collapses; redundant: statically indeterminate |
| Example: triangle ($j = 3$, $m = 3$) | Example: square of 4 bars ($m = 4 < 5$) or square with two diagonals ($m = 6 > 5$) |

Here $m$ = number of members and $j$ = number of joints.

items.path: library/archive/CE1103/Previous Year End Term Papers/End Term 2021-22 Sem 1.pdf
items.question_md: How would you distinguish between a deficient frame and a redundant frame?
items.answer_md:
Count the members $m$ and joints $j$ and compare with the perfect-frame condition $m = 2j - 3$:

- **Deficient frame:** $m < 2j - 3$. It has fewer members than needed, so it is unstable and changes shape (collapses) under load. Example: a square with 4 sides only ($4 < 5$).
- **Redundant frame:** $m > 2j - 3$. It has more members than needed, so it is stable but statically indeterminate; the forces cannot be found by $\sum F_x = 0$, $\sum F_y = 0$, $\sum M = 0$ alone. Example: a square with both diagonals ($6 > 5$).

Both are imperfect frames.

items.question_md:
A Truss of span 10 meters is loaded as shown in figure. Find the forces in all members of the truss.

[Figure: Truss with bottom chord A–E–B of span 10 m, supports at A and B. Members AC, CE, ED, DB, CD, AE, EB. Angle CAE = $60^\circ$, angle CEA = $60^\circ$, angle DEB = $60^\circ$, angle DBE = $30^\circ$. Vertical load 5 kN at C and 6 kN at D.]
items.answer_md:
**Geometry:** triangle ACE is equilateral ($60^\circ$, $60^\circ$); in triangle EDB, $\angle E = 60^\circ$, $\angle B = 30^\circ$, so $\angle D = 90^\circ$. With top chord CD horizontal (C and D at the same height), AE = $10/3$ = 3.333 m, so AC = CE = ED = CD = 3.333 m, EB = 6.667 m, DB = 5.774 m.
Coordinates (m): A(0, 0), E(3.333, 0), B(10, 0), C(1.667, 2.887), D(5.0, 2.887). Loads 5 kN at C, 6 kN at D. Tension positive.

**Reactions:** $\sum M_A = 0:\ R_B(10) = 5(1.667) + 6(5) = 38.33 \Rightarrow R_B = 3.833$ kN; $R_A = 11 - 3.833 = 7.167$ kN

**Joint A:** $F_{AC}\sin60^\circ + 7.167 = 0 \Rightarrow F_{AC} = -8.275$ kN (C); $F_{AE} = -F_{AC}\cos60^\circ = +4.138$ kN (T)

**Joint B:** $F_{DB}\sin30^\circ + 3.833 = 0 \Rightarrow F_{DB} = -7.667$ kN (C); $F_{EB} = -F_{DB}\cos30^\circ = +6.640$ kN (T)

**Joint C:** $\sum F_y:\ -F_{AC}\sin60^\circ - F_{CE}\sin60^\circ - 5 = 0 \Rightarrow F_{CE} = \dfrac{7.167 - 5}{0.866} = +2.502$ kN (T)
$\sum F_x:\ -0.5F_{AC} + 0.5F_{CE} + F_{CD} = 0 \Rightarrow F_{CD} = -4.138 - 1.251 = -5.389$ kN (C)

**Joint D:** $\sum F_y:\ -F_{ED}\sin60^\circ - F_{DB}\sin30^\circ - 6 = 0 \Rightarrow F_{ED} = \dfrac{3.833 - 6}{0.866} = -2.502$ kN (C)
Check $\sum F_x$ at D: $-F_{CD} - 0.5F_{ED} + 0.866F_{DB} = 5.389 + 1.251 - 6.640 = 0$ ✓

| Member | Force (kN) | Nature |
|---|---|---|
| AC | 8.275 | C |
| AE | 4.138 | T |
| CE | 2.502 | T |
| CD | 5.389 | C |
| ED | 2.502 | C |
| DB | 7.667 | C |
| EB | 6.640 | T |

items.question_md: What are the different types of beam? Explain with the neat sketches.
items.answer_md:
Beams are classified by their supports:

1. **Cantilever beam:** fixed at one end, free at the other. Sketch: beam built into a wall at the left, free at the right.
2. **Simply supported beam:** hinge at one end, roller at the other. Sketch: triangle under one end, circle under the other.
3. **Overhanging beam:** simply supported with one or both ends projecting beyond the supports.
4. **Fixed (built-in) beam:** both ends fixed.
5. **Propped cantilever:** one end fixed, the other simply supported.
6. **Continuous beam:** resting on more than two supports.

Cantilever, simply supported and overhanging beams are statically determinate; the rest are indeterminate.

items.path: library/archive/CE1103/Previous Year End Term Papers/End Term 2021-22 Sem 1.pdf
items.question_md: Define the term shear force and bending moment?
items.answer_md:
**Shear force** at a section is the algebraic sum of all vertical forces (loads and reactions) acting on either side of the section (unit: kN).

**Bending moment** at a section is the algebraic sum of the moments, about that section, of all forces acting on either side of it (unit: kN·m). Sagging BM is positive, hogging negative.

items.question_md:
Draw the shear force and bending moment diagram for the given beam. Also locate the point of contraflexure, if any.

[Figure: Beam ABC supported at A and B, AB = 4 m carrying UDL 10 kN/m, overhang BC = 2 m with 20 kN point load at free end C.]
items.answer_md:
Take $x$ from A: B at 4 m, C at 6 m. UDL 10 kN/m on AB, 20 kN at C.

**Reactions**

$\sum M_A = 0:\; 4R_B = 40(2) + 20(6) = 200 \Rightarrow R_B = 50$ kN

$R_A = 40 + 20 - 50 = 10$ kN

**Shear force**
- $V_A = +10$ kN; in AB, $V = 10 - 10x$, zero at $x = 1$ m
- Just left of B: $10 - 40 = -30$ kN; just right of B: $-30 + 50 = +20$ kN
- B to C: $+20$ kN

**Bending moment**
- $M_A = 0$
- At $x = 1$ m: $M = 10(1) - 5(1)^2 = 5$ kN·m (**maximum sagging**)
- $M_B = -20 \times 2 = -40$ kN·m (**maximum hogging**)
- $M_C = 0$

**Point of contraflexure:** $10x - 5x^2 = 0 \Rightarrow$ **$x = 2$ m from A**.

SFD: straight line from $+10$ at A through zero at 1 m to $-30$ at B, jump to $+20$, constant to C.
BMD: parabola from 0 up to 5 at 1 m, through zero at 2 m, down to $-40$ at B; straight line to 0 at C.

items.topic: Free body diagrams
items.question_md: Explain Free Body Diagram with suitable figure.
items.answer_md:
A **free body diagram** is a diagram of a body detached from all its supports and surrounding bodies, showing every external force on it: applied loads, its weight, and the reactions that replace the removed supports. It is the first step in applying the equations of equilibrium.

**Example (figure described):** a ladder leaning against a smooth wall on a rough floor. FBD: the ladder alone with W at its mid-point, the wall reaction $R_w$ horizontal, the floor reaction $R_f$ vertical upward, and friction F along the floor towards the wall.

items.topic: Equilibrium of rigid bodies in two and three dimensions
items.question_md:
The cylinder A of weight 4000 KN & B of weight 2000 KN resting on smooth inclined planes. They are connected by a bar of negligible weight hinged to each cylinder at their geometric centers by smooth pins. Find the force P, as shown in the figure that keeps the system in equilibrium.

[Figure: Large cylinder A rests in the corner between a smooth plane inclined at $60^\circ$ to the horizontal (left) and the horizontal floor. Smaller cylinder B rests in the corner between the floor and a smooth plane inclined at $45^\circ$ to the horizontal (right). A bar joins the centres of A and B, inclined at $15^\circ$ to the horizontal. Force P acts at the centre of B at $60^\circ$ to the vertical.]
items.answer_md:
**Reading of the figure:** the question says the cylinders rest on the smooth inclined planes, so each cylinder is taken to touch only its own plane (A on the $60^\circ$ plane, B on the $45^\circ$ plane); with floor contacts as well the problem would be statically indeterminate. The bar AB is at $15^\circ$ to the horizontal, the centre of the larger cylinder A being higher. P acts at the centre of B at $60^\circ$ to the vertical, directed downward towards A's side.

**Given:** $W_A = 4000$ kN, $W_B = 2000$ kN. Let C = force in the bar (compression).

### 1. Cylinder A: three concurrent forces
$W_A$ (vertical), $R_A$ (normal to the $60^\circ$ plane, i.e. $60^\circ$ to the vertical), C along the bar (pushing A away from B).

Resolving:
- Horizontal: $R_A\sin60^\circ = C\cos15^\circ$
- Vertical: $R_A\cos60^\circ + C\sin15^\circ = 4000$ (the bar descends from A to B, so its push on A has an upward component)

Solving: $C = \mathbf{4898.98\ kN}$ (compression), $R_A = 5464.10$ kN.

### 2. Cylinder B
Forces: $W_B = 2000$ kN down; $R_B$ normal to the $45^\circ$ plane (up and towards A); bar force C = 4898.98 kN pushing B away from A (to the right and downward at $15^\circ$); P at $60^\circ$ to the vertical (down and towards A).

- Horizontal: $-R_B\sin45^\circ - P\sin60^\circ + C\cos15^\circ = 0$
- Vertical: $R_B\cos45^\circ - P\cos60^\circ - C\sin15^\circ - 2000 = 0$

With $C\cos15^\circ = 4732.05$ and $C\sin15^\circ = 1267.95$:
$$0.7071R_B + 0.8660P = 4732.05$$
$$0.7071R_B - 0.5P = 3267.95$$
Subtracting: $1.3660P = 1464.10$
$$\boxed{P = 1071.8\ \text{kN}}$$
and $R_B = 5379.45$ kN.

**Answer:** $P = 1071.8$ kN (bar force 4898.98 kN compression, $R_A = 5464.10$ kN, $R_B = 5379.45$ kN). If P in your figure points upward and towards A at $60^\circ$ to the vertical, the same two equations with P reversed give $P = 4000$ kN.

items.topic: Moment of inertia of areas
items.question_md: Derive an expression for Moment of Inertia of a circle about its diametral axis.
items.answer_md:
Circle of radius $R$ (diameter $d=2R$). Take an elemental ring of radius $r$ and thickness $dr$: $dA=2\pi r\,dr$. Polar moment of inertia about the centre:
$$I_P=\int_0^R r^2(2\pi r\,dr)=\frac{\pi R^4}{2}$$
By symmetry $I_{xx}=I_{yy}$, and by the perpendicular axis theorem $I_P=I_{xx}+I_{yy}=2I_{xx}$:
$$\mathbf{I_{xx}=\frac{\pi R^4}{4}=\frac{\pi d^4}{64}}$$
where the x-axis is any diameter.

items.question_md:
Determine the Moment of Inertia of the shaded area as shown in figure about horizontal centroidal axis.

[Figure: Shaded semicircle of radius $R = 60$ mm with its diameter horizontal at the base. A rectangular notch 40 mm wide and 20 mm high is cut from the middle of the base, centred on the semicircle's centre.]
items.answer_md:
**Given:** semicircle of radius $R=60$ mm, diameter LM as base; rectangular cut-out 40 mm wide × 20 mm high from the middle of the base, symmetric about Y-Y.

**To find:** $I_{XX}$ about the horizontal centroidal axis.

**Step 1: Centroid** (y from base LM; $\bar x=0$ by symmetry)

| Part | Area (mm²) | $y$ (mm) | $a y$ (mm³) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Semicircle | $\frac{\pi(60)^2}{2}=5654.87$ | $\frac{4R}{3\pi}=25.465$ | 144000 |
| Rectangle (minus) | $-40\times20=-800$ | 10 | $-8000$ |
| **Net** | **4854.87** | | **136000** |

$$\bar y=\frac{136000}{4854.87}=28.01\ \text{mm above LM}$$

**Step 2: MI about the base LM**
- Semicircle: $\dfrac{\pi R^4}{8}=\dfrac{\pi(60)^4}{8}=5089380.1$ mm⁴
- Rectangle about its base: $\dfrac{bd^3}{3}=\dfrac{40\times20^3}{3}=106666.7$ mm⁴
$$I_{LM}=5089380.1-106666.7=4982713.4\ \text{mm}^4$$

**Step 3: Transfer to the centroidal axis**
$$I_{XX}=I_{LM}-A\bar y^2=4982713.4-4854.87\times28.01^2=4982713.4-3809785.3$$
$$\mathbf{I_{XX}=1.173\times10^6\ mm^4\ (1172928\ mm^4)}$$

items.path: library/archive/CE1103/Previous Year End Term Papers/End Term 2021-22 Sem 2.pdf
items.question_md: Explain various types of trusses with suitable sketches.
items.answer_md:
**By shape and arrangement of members (described sketches):**

| Truss | Sketch (described) | Use |
|---|---|---|
| **Pratt** | Parallel top and bottom chords, vertical members, diagonals sloping down towards the centre (diagonals in tension) | Bridges, roofs of medium span |
| **Howe** | Like Pratt but diagonals sloping up towards the centre (diagonals in compression, verticals in tension) | Timber bridges and roofs |
| **Warren** | Parallel chords joined by inclined members forming equilateral (or isosceles) triangles, no verticals | Bridges, gantries |
| **K-truss** | Verticals with two short diagonals meeting at mid-height of each vertical, forming a "K" | Long-span bridges |
| **Fink** | Triangular roof truss with the rafters subdivided by web members in a "W" pattern | Roofs of houses and sheds |
| **North-light (saw-tooth)** | Asymmetric triangle, one steep glazed face facing north | Factory roofs |
| **King-post / Queen-post** | Triangle with one central vertical (king post) or two verticals (queen posts) | Small roofs |

**By determinacy:** perfect ($m = 2j - 3$), deficient ($m < 2j - 3$) and redundant ($m > 2j - 3$) trusses.

**By plane:** plane trusses (all members in one plane) and space trusses (members in 3-D, e.g. transmission towers).

items.question_md:
A truss is loaded as shown in figure. Find out the magnitude & nature of forces in all the members of the truss and tabulate the results.

[Figure: Truss with bottom chord A–F–E–D, panels AF = FE = ED = 3 m. A is hinged and D is on rollers. B is 3 m above F, and C lies above E on line BD. Members: AB, BF, BC, CD, CE, FC, AF, FE, ED. Loads: horizontal 8 kN at B; 10 kN at each of B, C and D, acting normal to the top chord.]
items.answer_md:
**Geometry:** A(0, 0), F(3, 0), E(6, 0), D(9, 0); B(3, 3); C(6, 1.5) on BD (m).
AB at $45^\circ$ (4.243 m); BD slope 1/2 ($\sin\alpha = 0.447$, $\cos\alpha = 0.894$); BC = CD = FC = 3.354 m.
**Loads (as read from the figure):** 10 kN at B, C and D normal to BD, pressing on the roof, direction $(-0.447, -0.894)$, i.e. $(-4.472, -8.944)$ kN each; and 8 kN horizontal at B, taken to the right. A hinge, D roller. Tension positive.

**Reactions:**
$\sum F_x:\ H_A + 8 - 3(4.472) = 0 \Rightarrow H_A = 5.416$ kN (to the right)
$\sum M_A = 0:\ R_D(9) = 8.944(3 + 6 + 9) + 8(3) - 4.472(3 + 1.5) = 161.0 + 24 - 20.12 = 164.87$
$\Rightarrow R_D = 18.32$ kN; $\sum F_y:\ V_A = 26.83 - 18.32 = 8.51$ kN

**Joint D:** $\sum F_y:\ 0.447F_{CD} - 8.944 + 18.32 = 0 \Rightarrow F_{CD} = -20.96$ kN (C)

items.question_md: Classify the types of beams with suitable sketches.
items.answer_md:
Beams are classified by their supports:

1. **Cantilever beam:** fixed at one end, free at the other. Sketch: beam built into a wall at the left, free at the right.
2. **Simply supported beam:** hinge at one end, roller at the other. Sketch: triangle under one end, circle under the other.
3. **Overhanging beam:** simply supported with one or both ends projecting beyond the supports.
4. **Fixed (built-in) beam:** both ends fixed.
5. **Propped cantilever:** one end fixed, the other simply supported.
6. **Continuous beam:** resting on more than two supports.

Cantilever, simply supported and overhanging beams are statically determinate; the rest are indeterminate.

items.question_md: Explain Poisson's ratio with suitable figure.
items.answer_md:
**Poisson's ratio ($\mu$ or $\nu$)** is the ratio of lateral strain to longitudinal strain when a body is stressed within the elastic limit:
$$\mu = \frac{\text{lateral strain}}{\text{longitudinal strain}} = \frac{\delta d/d}{\delta L/L}$$
**Figure:** a bar of length $L$ and diameter $d$ under axial tension $P$ elongates by $\delta L$ and its diameter decreases by $\delta d$. (Under compression it shortens and bulges.) For most metals $\mu = 0.25$ to $0.33$; its upper limit for isotropic materials is 0.5.

items.question_md:
A member ABCD is subjected to point loads $P_1$, $P_2$, $P_3$ and $P_4$ as shown in figure. Calculate the force $P_2$ necessary for equilibrium, if $P_1 = 45$ kN, $P_3 = 450$ kN, and $P_4 = 130$ kN. Determine the total elongation of the member, assuming the modulus of elasticity to be $2.1 \times 10^5\ \text{N/mm}^2$.

[Figure: Stepped bar. AB has area $625\ \text{mm}^2$ and length 120 cm; BC has area $2500\ \text{mm}^2$ and length 60 cm; CD has area $1250\ \text{mm}^2$ and length 90 cm. $P_1$ acts leftward at A, $P_2$ rightward at B, $P_3$ leftward at C, and $P_4$ rightward at D.]
items.answer_md:
**Given:** $P_1 = 45$ kN (left, at A), $P_3 = 450$ kN (left, at C), $P_4 = 130$ kN (right, at D), $E = 2.1 \times 10^5$ N/mm$^2$.

| Part | Area (mm²) | Length (mm) |
|---|---|---|
| AB | 625 | 1200 |
| BC | 2500 | 600 |
| CD | 1250 | 900 |

**1. Force $P_2$** (rightward positive): $-45 + P_2 - 450 + 130 = 0$
$$\boxed{P_2 = 365 \text{ kN (to the right)}}$$

**2. Internal forces** (free body left of each cut)
- AB: 45 kN tension
- BC: $-45 + 365 = 320$ kN pushing: **320 kN compression**
- CD: $320 - 450 = -130$: **130 kN tension** (balances $P_4$)

**3. Stresses:** $\sigma_{AB} = 45000/625 = 72$ N/mm² (T); $\sigma_{BC} = 320000/2500 = 128$ N/mm² (C); $\sigma_{CD} = 130000/1250 = 104$ N/mm² (T)

**4. Changes in length** $\delta = PL/AE$:
- $\delta_{AB} = \dfrac{45000 \times 1200}{625 \times 2.1\times10^5} = +0.4114$ mm
- $\delta_{BC} = -\dfrac{320000 \times 600}{2500 \times 2.1\times10^5} = -0.3657$ mm
- $\delta_{CD} = \dfrac{130000 \times 900}{1250 \times 2.1\times10^5} = +0.4457$ mm

**Total elongation** $= 0.4114 - 0.3657 + 0.4457 = \mathbf{0.4914\ mm}$

items.question_md: Derive the expression for the relation between modulus of elasticity and modulus of Rigidity, $E = 2C(1+\mu)$, with usual notations.
items.answer_md:
Take a square block of side $a$ under pure shear stress $\tau$; shear strain $\phi = \tau/C$, top displacement $\delta = a\phi$.

- Geometry: diagonal $a\sqrt2$ lengthens by $\delta\cos45^\circ$, so $\varepsilon_d = \dfrac{a\phi/\sqrt2}{a\sqrt2} = \dfrac{\phi}{2} = \dfrac{\tau}{2C}$.
- Stresses: pure shear gives tension $\tau$ along this diagonal and compression $\tau$ across it, so $\varepsilon_d = \dfrac{\tau}{E}(1 + \mu)$.

Equating: $\dfrac{\tau}{2C} = \dfrac{\tau}{E}(1+\mu) \Rightarrow \boxed{E = 2C(1+\mu)}$

items.topic: Parallel axis theorem
items.question_md: State and prove Parallel Axes Theorem for Moment of Inertia.
items.answer_md:
**Statement:** MI of an area about any axis = MI about a parallel centroidal axis + area × (distance between axes)²: $I_{AB}=I_G+Ah^2$.

**Proof:** an element $dA$ at distance $y$ from G-G is at $(h+y)$ from A-B:
$$I_{AB}=\int(h+y)^2dA=h^2\!\int dA+2h\!\int y\,dA+\int y^2dA=Ah^2+0+I_G$$
since $\int y\,dA=0$ (first moment about the centroidal axis). Hence $\mathbf{I_{AB}=I_G+Ah^2}$.

items.topic: Composition of concurrent forces in a plane
items.question_md: State and prove Lami's theorem with suitable figure.
items.answer_md: **Lami's theorem:** if three coplanar concurrent forces P, Q, R are in equilibrium, $\dfrac{P}{\sin\alpha}=\dfrac{Q}{\sin\beta}=\dfrac{R}{\sin\gamma}$, where $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ are the angles opposite P, Q, R. *Proof:* the forces form a closed triangle with interior angles $180^\circ-\alpha$, $180^\circ-\beta$, $180^\circ-\gamma$; the sine rule and $\sin(180^\circ-\theta)=\sin\theta$ give the result.

items.topic: Free body diagrams
items.question_md: Explain the concept of free body diagram with neat sketches.
items.answer_md:
A **free body diagram (FBD)** is a sketch of a body (or part of it) isolated from its surroundings, on which **all external forces** acting on it are shown: applied loads, self-weight, and the reactions that replace every support or contact.

**Steps:** isolate the body; show weight at the centre of gravity; replace each support or contact by its reaction (smooth surface: normal force; string: tension away from the body; hinge: $H$ and $V$; fixed end: $H$, $V$, $M$); mark dimensions and angles.

**Sketch (in words):** a sphere resting against a smooth wall held by a string. FBD: the sphere alone, with W vertically down at the centre, the wall reaction R horizontal away from the wall, and tension T along the string towards its support; all three meet at the centre.

items.question_md: State the principle of transmissibility of forces.
items.answer_md: **Principle of transmissibility:** if a force acts at a point on a rigid body, it may be considered to act at any other point **on its line of action** without changing the external effect (equilibrium or motion) of the body. Example: pushing a cart at the back or pulling it with the same force at the front along the same line gives the same motion.

items.question_md: A particle is acted upon by three forces, equal to 20 N, 35 N and 10 N along three sides of an equilibrium triangle, taken in order. Find graphically or otherwise the magnitude and direction of the resultant force.
items.answer_md:
**Given:** forces 20 N, 35 N, 10 N along the three sides of an equilateral triangle, taken in order. Taken in order, the forces are inclined at $0^\circ$, $120^\circ$, $240^\circ$ (each side turns the direction by the exterior angle $120^\circ$).

**To find:** magnitude and direction of the resultant.

**Analytical method** (x-axis along the 20 N force):
$$\Sigma F_x=20+35\cos120^\circ+10\cos240^\circ=20-17.5-5=-2.5\ \text{N}$$
$$\Sigma F_y=0+35\sin120^\circ+10\sin240^\circ=30.311-8.660=21.651\ \text{N}$$
$$R=\sqrt{(-2.5)^2+21.651^2}=\sqrt{475}=\mathbf{21.79\ N}$$
$$\tan\alpha=\frac{21.651}{2.5}\Rightarrow\alpha=83.41^\circ$$
Since $\Sigma F_x$ is negative and $\Sigma F_y$ positive, R lies in the second quadrant:
**R = 21.79 N at $96.59^\circ$ to the direction of the 20 N force** (i.e. $83.41^\circ$ to the reverse of the 20 N force, towards the 35 N side).

**Check by the short method:** three equal forces along the sides of an equilateral triangle taken in order are in equilibrium, so subtract 10 N from each: the system reduces to 10 N and 25 N at $120^\circ$:
$$R=\sqrt{10^2+25^2+2(10)(25)\cos120^\circ}=\sqrt{475}=21.79\ \text{N}\ \checkmark$$

**Graphical method:** draw the 20, 35, 10 N vectors head to tail to a scale at $0^\circ$, $120^\circ$, $240^\circ$; the closing line from the start to the end of the polygon measures about 21.8 N at about $96.6^\circ$ to the first force.

items.topic: Vector operations
items.question_md:
Explain briefly the following:

(i) Paralleogram law of forces.

(ii) Characteristics of forces.
items.answer_md:
### (i) Parallelogram law of forces
If two forces acting at a point are represented in magnitude and direction by the two adjacent sides of a parallelogram, their resultant is represented in magnitude and direction by the diagonal of the parallelogram that passes through that point.

For forces P and Q at angle $\theta$:
$$R = \sqrt{P^2 + Q^2 + 2PQ\cos\theta},\qquad \tan\alpha = \frac{Q\sin\theta}{P + Q\cos\theta}$$
where $\alpha$ is the angle of R with P.

**Example:** $P = 3$ N and $Q = 4$ N at $90^\circ$: $R = \sqrt{9+16} = 5$ N, $\alpha = \tan^{-1}(4/3) = 53.13^\circ$ with P.

### (ii) Characteristics of a force
A force is completely specified by four characteristics:
1. **Magnitude:** its size, in newtons (N) or kN.
2. **Direction:** the angle its line of action makes with a reference axis.
3. **Sense (nature):** push or pull, shown by the arrowhead along the line.
4. **Point of application:** the point of the body where it acts.

Force is therefore a vector quantity; its line of action is the line along which it acts.

items.question_md:
A bar 4 m long and of negligible weight is acted upon by a vertical load of 400 N and a horizontal load of 200 N applied at positions as shown in fig.. The ends of the bar are in contact with a smooth vertical wall and a smooth incline. Determine the equilibrium position of the bar as defined by the angle $\theta$, it makes with the horizontal.

[Figure: Bar AB inclined at angle $\theta$ to the horizontal, end A against a smooth vertical wall with horizontal reaction $N_A$, end B on a smooth incline at $45^\circ$ with reaction $N_B$ at $45^\circ$. Along the bar from A: 1 m to the vertical 400 N load, then 2 m to the point where the horizontal 200 N load acts (pointing towards the wall), then 1 m to B.]
items.answer_md:
**Given:** weightless bar AB = 4 m; A on a smooth vertical wall ($N_A$ horizontal); B on a smooth $45^\circ$ incline ($N_B$ at $45^\circ$ to the vertical); 400 N vertical at 1 m from A; 200 N horizontal (towards the wall) at 3 m from A.

### 1. Force equations
$\sum F_y = 0$: $N_B\cos45^\circ = 400 \Rightarrow N_B = 565.69$ N, so its horizontal component is 400 N (towards the wall).

$\sum F_x = 0$: $N_A = 200 + 400 = 600$ N (away from the wall).

### 2. Moment equation about A
Let A be the upper end and $\theta$ the angle of the bar with the horizontal. Coordinates from A: a point at distance $s$ along the bar is $(s\cos\theta,\ -s\sin\theta)$.

- 400 N at $s = 1$: moment $= 400 \times 1\cos\theta$ (clockwise)
- 200 N at $s = 3$: moment $= 200 \times 3\sin\theta$ (clockwise)
- $N_B$ at $s = 4$: vertical part $400 \times 4\cos\theta$ (anticlockwise), horizontal part $400 \times 4\sin\theta$ (clockwise)

$$1600\cos\theta - 1600\sin\theta - 400\cos\theta - 600\sin\theta = 0$$
$$1200\cos\theta = 2200\sin\theta \Rightarrow \tan\theta = \frac{12}{22} = 0.5455$$
$$\boxed{\theta = 28.61^\circ}$$

**Answer:** the bar rests at $\theta = 28.61^\circ$ to the horizontal, with $N_A = 600$ N and $N_B = 565.69$ N.

items.topic: Centroid of areas
items.question_md: Explain the various methods to determine the centre of gravity with examples.
items.answer_md:
**Centre of gravity (C.G.)**: the point through which the resultant of the weights of all particles of a body acts, whatever the orientation of the body. For a plane area the corresponding point is the **centroid**.

**Methods of determining the C.G.**

1. **By geometrical considerations (symmetry):** if a body has an axis of symmetry, the C.G. lies on it; with two axes it lies at their intersection.
   *Examples:* rectangle, at the intersection of diagonals ($b/2,\ d/2$); circle, at its centre; triangle, at the intersection of medians, $h/3$ from the base.
2. **By moments (method of moments / composite sections):** divide the body into simple parts of known areas $a_i$ and centroids $(x_i, y_i)$ and take moments about reference axes:
   $$\bar x=\frac{\sum a_i x_i}{\sum a_i},\qquad \bar y=\frac{\sum a_i y_i}{\sum a_i}$$
   (holes are taken with negative area). *Example:* T-section, L-section, I-section.
3. **By integration:** for areas bounded by curves, take an elemental strip $dA$:
   $$\bar x=\frac{\int x\,dA}{\int dA},\qquad \bar y=\frac{\int y\,dA}{\int dA}$$
   *Example:* semicircle, $\bar y=4r/3\pi$; quarter circle; area under a parabola.
4. **Graphical method:** the areas (or weights) are drawn as parallel forces; using the force polygon and funicular (link) polygon in two directions, the line of action of the resultant is found each time; their intersection is the C.G. Used for irregular sections.
5. **Experimental (suspension / plumb-line) method:** a lamina is hung freely from two different points and a vertical line is marked each time with a plumb line; the intersection of the two lines is the C.G. *Example:* irregular cardboard lamina.

items.path: library/archive/CE1103/Previous Year End Term Papers/End Term 2022-23 Sem 1.pdf
items.question_md:
Explain briefly the following:
\ni) Signifince of SFD and BMD.

ii) Characteristics of Couples.
items.answer_md:
### i) Significance of SFD and BMD
1. They show the SF and BM at every section of the beam at a glance.
2. The maximum BM (where SF is zero or changes sign) gives the maximum bending stress, which fixes the size of the section.
3. The maximum SF gives the maximum shear stress, used for web and shear-reinforcement design.
4. The BMD shows points of contraflexure, where reinforcement in RCC must change face and where joints are best located.
5. They are needed to compute slope and deflection (e.g. moment-area method).

### ii) Characteristics of a couple
1. A couple is two equal, parallel, unlike forces with different lines of action; its resultant force is zero.
2. Its moment $= F \times d$ ($d$ = arm) is the same about every point in its plane.
3. It produces only rotation, not translation.
4. A couple can be balanced only by an equal and opposite couple, not by a single force.
5. It can be moved anywhere in its plane, and $F$ and $d$ can be changed, without any change in effect as long as $F \times d$ and the sense are unchanged.

items.question_md: Enlist the different types of trusses with neat sketches.
items.answer_md:
**By shape and arrangement of members (described sketches):**

| Truss | Sketch (described) | Use |
|---|---|---|
| **Pratt** | Parallel top and bottom chords, vertical members, diagonals sloping down towards the centre (diagonals in tension) | Bridges, roofs of medium span |
| **Howe** | Like Pratt but diagonals sloping up towards the centre (diagonals in compression, verticals in tension) | Timber bridges and roofs |
| **Warren** | Parallel chords joined by inclined members forming equilateral (or isosceles) triangles, no verticals | Bridges, gantries |
| **K-truss** | Verticals with two short diagonals meeting at mid-height of each vertical, forming a "K" | Long-span bridges |
| **Fink** | Triangular roof truss with the rafters subdivided by web members in a "W" pattern | Roofs of houses and sheds |
| **North-light (saw-tooth)** | Asymmetric triangle, one steep glazed face facing north | Factory roofs |
| **King-post / Queen-post** | Triangle with one central vertical (king post) or two verticals (queen posts) | Small roofs |

**By determinacy:** perfect ($m = 2j - 3$), deficient ($m < 2j - 3$) and redundant ($m > 2j - 3$) trusses.

**By plane:** plane trusses (all members in one plane) and space trusses (members in 3-D, e.g. transmission towers).

items.question_md: What do you understand by determinate structures.
items.answer_md:
A **statically determinate structure** is one whose support reactions and internal forces can all be found from the **equations of static equilibrium alone**:
$$\sum F_x = 0, \quad \sum F_y = 0, \quad \sum M = 0$$
The number of unknowns equals the number of available equations. Examples: simply supported beam, cantilever, perfect truss ($m + r = 2j$, i.e. $m = 2j - 3$ with three reaction components). If unknowns exceed equations the structure is **indeterminate** (e.g. fixed beam, redundant truss).

items.topic: Moment of inertia of areas
items.question_md: Explain moment of inertia and polar moment of inertia.
items.answer_md:
**Moment of inertia (second moment of area)**

The moment of inertia of a plane area about an axis in its plane is the sum of the products of each elemental area and the square of its distance from that axis:
$$I_{xx}=\int y^2\,dA,\qquad I_{yy}=\int x^2\,dA$$
- Units: $\text{mm}^4$, $\text{cm}^4$, $\text{m}^4$; always positive.
- It measures the resistance of a section to bending about that axis (used in the flexure formula $M/I=\sigma/y$ and in deflection).
- Radius of gyration: $k=\sqrt{I/A}$.
- *Example:* rectangle $b\times d$: $I_{xx}=\dfrac{bd^3}{12}$ about its horizontal centroidal axis.

**Polar moment of inertia**

The moment of inertia of a plane area about an axis **perpendicular** to its plane (passing through a point O, the pole) is
$$I_P=J=\int r^2\,dA$$
where $r$ is the distance of $dA$ from the pole. Since $r^2=x^2+y^2$,
$$I_P=I_{xx}+I_{yy}\quad(\text{perpendicular axis theorem})$$
- It measures the resistance of a section to twisting (used in the torsion formula $T/J=\tau/r$).
- *Example:* solid circular shaft of diameter $d$: $I_P=\dfrac{\pi d^4}{32}=2\times\dfrac{\pi d^4}{64}$.

items.topic: Moment of inertia of composite areas
items.question_md:
Find the moment of inertia and radius of gyration of the area shown in Fig. about the axis AB.

[Figure: Composite area: rectangle (2) of width 10 + 30 + 10 = 50 mm and height 20 mm below axis AB (AB along its top edge); triangle (1) of height 15 mm above AB on the rectangle's top edge; semicircle (3) of radius 15 mm cut out from the bottom edge of the rectangle, centred with 10 mm on each side.]
items.answer_md:
**Given (mm):** (1) triangle, base 50 on AB, height 15 above AB; (2) rectangle 50 × 20 below AB, AB along its top edge; (3) semicircle $r=15$ cut from the bottom edge of the rectangle (diameter on the bottom edge, 10 mm from each side).

**To find:** $I_{AB}$ and $k_{AB}$.

**Part (1) Triangle, base on AB:**
$$I_1=\frac{bh^3}{12}=\frac{50\times15^3}{12}=14062.5\ \text{mm}^4,\quad a_1=375\ \text{mm}^2$$

**Part (2) Rectangle, top edge on AB:**
$$I_2=\frac{bd^3}{3}=\frac{50\times20^3}{3}=133333.33\ \text{mm}^4,\quad a_2=1000\ \text{mm}^2$$

**Part (3) Semicircle (to subtract):**
- $a_3=\dfrac{\pi(15)^2}{2}=353.43$ mm²; its centroid is $\dfrac{4r}{3\pi}=6.366$ mm above the bottom edge, so $h=20-6.366=13.634$ mm below AB
- $I_G=\dfrac{\pi r^4}{8}-a_3(6.366)^2=19880.39-14323.94=5556.45$ mm⁴
- $I_3=I_G+a_3h^2=5556.45+353.43\times13.634^2=5556.45+65695.61=71252.06$ mm⁴

**Moment of inertia about AB**
$$I_{AB}=14062.5+133333.33-71252.06=\mathbf{76143.8\ mm^4}$$

**Radius of gyration**
$$A=375+1000-353.43=1021.57\ \text{mm}^2$$
$$k_{AB}=\sqrt{\frac{I_{AB}}{A}}=\sqrt{\frac{76143.8}{1021.57}}=\mathbf{8.63\ mm}$$

items.topic: Composition of concurrent forces in a plane
items.question_md: State and prove Lami's theorem with suitable figure.
items.answer_md:
**Statement:** If three coplanar concurrent forces acting on a particle keep it in equilibrium, each force is proportional to the sine of the angle between the other two:
$$\frac{P}{\sin\alpha}=\frac{Q}{\sin\beta}=\frac{R}{\sin\gamma}$$
where $\alpha$ is the angle between Q and R, $\beta$ between R and P, $\gamma$ between P and Q.

**Figure (described):** forces P, Q, R act at point O; $\alpha$ is opposite P, $\beta$ opposite Q, $\gamma$ opposite R.

**Proof:**
1. Since the three forces are in equilibrium, they can be represented by the three sides of a triangle taken in order (triangle law). Draw $ab\parallel P$, $bc\parallel Q$, $ca\parallel R$.
2. The interior angles of this triangle are the supplements of the angles between the forces:
   angle opposite $ab$ (P) $=180^\circ-\alpha$, opposite $bc$ (Q) $=180^\circ-\beta$, opposite $ca$ (R) $=180^\circ-\gamma$.
3. By the sine rule for triangle abc:
$$\frac{ab}{\sin(180^\circ-\alpha)}=\frac{bc}{\sin(180^\circ-\beta)}=\frac{ca}{\sin(180^\circ-\gamma)}$$
4. Since $\sin(180^\circ-\theta)=\sin\theta$ and $ab, bc, ca$ represent P, Q, R:
$$\mathbf{\frac{P}{\sin\alpha}=\frac{Q}{\sin\beta}=\frac{R}{\sin\gamma}}$$

*Use:* finding two unknown forces when three concurrent forces keep a body in equilibrium (e.g. tensions in two strings supporting a weight).

items.topic: Planar force systems
items.question_md: Four forces $5P$, $10P$, $12P$ and $15P$ act along four sides of a square 200 mm taken in order. Find the magnitude and position of the resultant force.
items.answer_md:
**Given:** square ABCD of side $a = 200$ mm. Forces taken in order: $5P$ along AB, $10P$ along BC, $12P$ along CD, $15P$ along DA.

**Axes:** origin at A, AB along +x, AD along +y: A(0, 0), B(200, 0), C(200, 200), D(0, 200).

### 1. Resolution
$$\sum F_x = 5P - 12P = -7P,\qquad \sum F_y = 10P - 15P = -5P$$
$$R = \sqrt{(7P)^2 + (5P)^2} = \sqrt{74}\,P = \mathbf{8.60P}$$
$$\theta = \tan^{-1}\frac{5}{7} = \mathbf{35.54^\circ}$$ with AB, the resultant acting downward and towards the left (third quadrant).

### 2. Moment about A (anticlockwise positive)
AB and DA pass through A.
$$\sum M_A = 10P \times 200 + 12P \times 200 = 4400P\ \text{N·mm (anticlockwise)}$$

### 3. Position
Perpendicular distance from A:
$$d = \frac{4400P}{8.602P} = \mathbf{511.5\ mm}$$
Intercept on line AB: $x \cdot \sum F_y = \sum M_A \Rightarrow x = \dfrac{4400P}{-5P} = -880$ mm, i.e. the resultant cuts **AB produced at 880 mm from A on the side away from B**.

items.topic: Classification of force systems
items.question_md: Explain the classification of forces.
items.answer_md:
Forces (force systems) are classified by the position of their lines of action:

1. **Coplanar forces:** lines of action lie in one plane.
   - **Collinear:** all along one common line. Example: forces in a rope in tug of war.
   - **Concurrent:** lines of action meet at one point. Example: forces at a joint of a truss.
   - **Parallel:** lines of action are parallel. *Like* parallel (same sense) or *unlike* (opposite sense). Example: loads and reactions on a beam under vertical loads.
   - **Non-concurrent, non-parallel (general):** neither meet at a point nor are parallel. Example: forces on a ladder against a wall.
2. **Non-coplanar forces:** lines of action do not lie in one plane.
   - **Concurrent:** meet at a point. Example: forces in the legs of a tripod.
   - **Parallel:** Example: weights on a table and the reactions at its four legs.
   - **Non-concurrent, non-parallel:** general space forces. Example: forces on a crane or a shaft.

Forces may also be classed as **external** (applied loads, reactions) and **internal** (forces in members), or as **contact** and **body (non-contact)** forces such as weight.

items.topic: Free body diagrams
items.question_md:
Two cylinders '1' and '2' rest in a horizontal channel as shown in Fig. 2.45. The cylinder '1' has a weight of 250 N and radius of 180 mm. The cylinder '2' has a weight of 200 N and a radius of 100 mm. The channel is 360 mm wide at the bottom with one side vertical. The other side is inclined at an angle $60^\circ$ with the horizontal. Find the reactions.

[Figure: Cylinder 1 (radius 180 mm, weight 250 N) rests on the channel bottom MO at N (reaction $R_N$) and against the left side inclined at $60^\circ$ at L (reaction $R_L$). Cylinder 2 (radius 100 mm, weight 200 N) sits above and to the right, touching cylinder 1 at Q (reaction $R_Q$) and the vertical right wall at P (reaction $R_P$). Bottom corners M and O.]
items.answer_md:
**Given:** cylinder 1: $W_1 = 250$ N, $r_1 = 180$ mm; cylinder 2: $W_2 = 200$ N, $r_2 = 100$ mm. Channel bottom MO = 360 mm, side at M inclined at $60^\circ$ to the horizontal, side at O vertical.

### 1. Geometry (origin at M, x along MO)
- Centre $O_1$ is 180 mm above the bottom and 180 mm from the $60^\circ$ side. Distance from M along the bottom to the foot of $O_1$: $\dfrac{180(1 - \cos60^\circ)}{\sin60^\circ} = \dfrac{90}{0.866} = 103.92$ mm. So $O_1 = (103.92,\ 180)$.
- Centre $O_2$ is 100 mm from the vertical wall: $x_2 = 360 - 100 = 260$ mm.
- $O_1O_2 = r_1 + r_2 = 280$ mm. Horizontal gap $= 260 - 103.92 = 156.08$ mm.
$$\cos\theta = \frac{156.08}{280} \Rightarrow \theta = 56.12^\circ\ \text{(line of centres with the horizontal)}$$

### 2. Cylinder 2: forces $W_2$, $R_P$ (horizontal), $R_Q$ along $O_1O_2$
$$R_Q\sin\theta = 200 \Rightarrow R_Q = \frac{200}{\sin56.12^\circ} = \mathbf{240.90\ N}$$
$$R_P = R_Q\cos\theta = \mathbf{134.28\ N}$$

### 3. Cylinder 1: forces $W_1$, $R_Q$ (from 2), $R_L$ (normal to the $60^\circ$ side, at $30^\circ$ to the horizontal), $R_N$ (vertical)
$$\sum F_x = 0:\ R_L\cos30^\circ = R_Q\cos\theta = 134.28 \Rightarrow R_L = \mathbf{155.05\ N}$$
$$\sum F_y = 0:\ R_N + R_L\sin30^\circ = 250 + R_Q\sin\theta = 450$$
$$R_N = 450 - 77.53 = \mathbf{372.47\ N}$$

**Answer:** $R_P = 134.28$ N, $R_Q = 240.90$ N, $R_L = 155.05$ N, $R_N = 372.47$ N.

items.topic: Moment of inertia of areas
items.question_md: Derive the expression for Moment of Inertia of a circular lamina about its diameter.
items.answer_md:
**Circular lamina** of radius $R$ (diameter $d$), centre O; x-axis along a diameter.

**Method 1: direct integration with a horizontal strip**

A strip parallel to the x-axis at distance $y$, thickness $dy$, has width $2\sqrt{R^2-y^2}$. Put $y=R\sin\theta$, $dy=R\cos\theta\,d\theta$:
$$I_{xx}=\int_{-R}^{R}y^2\cdot2\sqrt{R^2-y^2}\,dy=2\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}R^2\sin^2\theta\cdot R\cos\theta\cdot R\cos\theta\,d\theta$$
$$=2R^4\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\sin^2\theta\cos^2\theta\,d\theta=\frac{R^4}{2}\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\sin^22\theta\,d\theta=\frac{R^4}{2}\cdot\frac{\pi}{2}=\frac{\pi R^4}{4}$$

**Method 2 (check): polar moment and perpendicular axis theorem**

Elemental ring of radius $r$, thickness $dr$: $dA=2\pi r\,dr$
$$I_P=\int_0^R r^2\,2\pi r\,dr=\frac{\pi R^4}{2}$$
By symmetry $I_{xx}=I_{yy}$, and $I_P=I_{xx}+I_{yy}$, so $I_{xx}=\frac{I_P}{2}$.

**Result:**
$$\mathbf{I_{diameter}=\frac{\pi R^4}{4}=\frac{\pi d^4}{64}}$$
